overview: The Databricks Control Plane is the Databricks-managed backend, hosted in Databricks' own cloud account, that provides the workspace UI, notebooks, job scheduler, cluster manager, and metadata services.
It orchestrates and manages compute resources that run in the customer's environment (the data plane) without, in the classic architecture, holding the customer's actual data.
Understanding the control-plane/data-plane split is foundational to Databricks security, networking, and architecture, and is a frequent interview topic.
learningObjectives: Understand exactly which Databricks services live in the control plane versus the customer's cloud account.
Explain how the control plane orchestrates compute in the data plane without (mostly) accessing customer data.
Describe the security boundary between control plane and data plane and the implications for compliance.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The Control Plane is the set of Databricks-managed backend services running in Databricks' cloud account that handle workspace management, notebook storage, job orchestration, cluster lifecycle management, and metadata (such as cluster configurations, notebook commands, and user identity). It issues commands to compute resources running in the data plane via a secure relay, while customer data is processed and stored in the data plane (classic) or in a Databricks-managed serverless environment (serverless).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of the control plane as the 'cockpit' of Databricks: it is the website you log into, where you write notebooks, schedule jobs, and click 'start cluster.' The actual heavy lifting of crunching your data happens elsewhere (the data plane). The cockpit sends instructions to the engine room but, in classic deployments, the cockpit never touches the raw fuel (your data) directly.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Databricks pioneered the control-plane/data-plane separation to address enterprise security concerns about a SaaS vendor having access to sensitive data. By keeping the classic data plane inside the customer's own cloud account (AWS VPC, Azure VNet, or GCP project), Databricks could offer a managed experience while letting customers retain control and ownership of their data. This model evolved with the introduction of serverless compute (~2021 onward), which shifted some compute into a Databricks-managed environment.

whyItMatters.business: The split lets enterprises adopt a fully managed analytics platform while satisfying data residency, sovereignty, and compliance requirements (HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR) because customer data largely stays in their own account.
whyItMatters.engineering: Engineers must configure networking (VPC peering, private link, security groups) between the control plane and data plane; understanding the boundary is essential for debugging connectivity, secrets management, and cluster startup failures.
whyItMatters.scalability: The control plane centrally manages cluster autoscaling, job queuing, and metadata for thousands of workspaces, while elastic compute scales independently in the data plane, decoupling orchestration from raw processing capacity.
whyItMatters.cost: Control plane services are part of the Databricks platform; customers pay for compute (DBUs) plus the underlying cloud VMs/storage in the data plane. Understanding the split clarifies the Databricks bill versus the cloud-provider bill.
whyItMatters.reliability: Databricks operates the control plane with high availability and regional redundancy. If the control plane is unreachable, running clusters may continue processing but new orchestration (job launches, autoscaling) is impacted, so engineers must understand failure domains.

coreComponents.name: Workspace UI and Notebooks
coreComponents.definition: The web application and REST/UI layer where users author notebooks, browse data, and manage the workspace; notebook source and command history are stored in the control plane.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide the interactive authoring and collaboration surface for data engineering, analytics, and ML.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Stores notebook code, revision history, dashboards, and workspace objects; routes user commands to the appropriate cluster.
coreComponents.examples: The Databricks web UI at <workspace>.cloud.databricks.com; notebook autosave and Repos Git integration.

coreComponents.name: Cluster Manager
coreComponents.definition: The control-plane service that manages the lifecycle of clusters (create, start, resize, autoscale, terminate) by calling the cloud provider's compute APIs in the customer account.
coreComponents.purpose: To provision and tear down the compute (VMs) that form the data plane on demand.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Requests/releases cloud VM instances, applies cluster configuration and instance profiles/managed identities, manages autoscaling decisions.
coreComponents.examples: Starting an all-purpose cluster, autoscaling a job cluster from 2 to 8 workers, terminating idle clusters.

coreComponents.name: Job Scheduler (Workflows)
coreComponents.definition: The orchestration service that triggers jobs on schedules, via APIs, or on events, manages task dependencies (DAGs), retries, and tracks run history.
coreComponents.purpose: To run production pipelines reliably without manual intervention.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Maintains job definitions and run metadata, launches job clusters, enforces dependencies and retry policies, records logs/metrics.
coreComponents.examples: A daily ETL Workflow with task dependencies, a retry-on-failure policy, and alerting on failure.

internalWorking: A user action in the UI (e.g., 'run cell' or 'start cluster') is received by control-plane services, which authenticate the user, check permissions, and persist relevant metadata.

For cluster operations, the cluster manager calls the cloud provider's compute API in the customer's account to launch VMs; each VM runs a Databricks agent that establishes a secure outbound connection back to the control plane (via a secure cluster connectivity relay).

Notebook commands and results are routed through the control plane to the cluster over this secure channel; in classic compute, the actual data read/written stays within the data plane and customer cloud storage, while only commands, results metadata, and small previews transit the control plane.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: User -> Control Plane (UI, scheduler, cluster manager, metadata) -> secure relay -> Data Plane (clusters/VMs in customer cloud) -> Cloud Storage (customer account)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A user logs into the workspace UI (control plane) and is authenticated via the configured identity provider/SSO.
2. The user starts a cluster; the cluster manager (control plane) calls the cloud compute API to launch VMs in the customer's VPC/VNet (data plane).
3. Each cluster VM boots the Databricks runtime and opens a secure outbound connection to the control plane relay (Secure Cluster Connectivity), so no inbound ports need to be open.

4. The user runs a notebook cell; the command travels control plane -> relay -> driver node, which reads data directly from customer cloud storage and returns only results/previews back through the relay to the UI.

keyTerminology.meaning: Databricks-managed backend services (UI, notebooks, scheduler, cluster manager, metadata) hosted in Databricks' cloud account.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines what Databricks manages and where orchestration and metadata live.

keyTerminology.meaning: Where compute runs and data is processed; in classic architecture this is the customer's own cloud account.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines where customer data is actually handled, central to the security model.

keyTerminology.term: Secure Cluster Connectivity (SCC) / No Public IP
keyTerminology.meaning: A networking mode where data-plane clusters have only outbound connectivity to the control plane via a relay, with no public IPs and no open inbound ports.
keyTerminology.importance: Reduces attack surface; a common enterprise hardening requirement.

importantConcepts.explanation: The control plane stores metadata (notebook code, cluster configs, job definitions, run history, table/schema metadata via the metastore) but, in classic compute, does not store or process the actual rows of customer data, which remain in the data plane and customer cloud storage.

Enterprises can deploy the classic data plane into a VPC/VNet they own and control, applying their own security groups, subnets, and egress controls, while the control plane remains Databricks-managed.

variationsAndTypes: **Multi-tenant Control Plane:** The default; Databricks operates a shared control plane per region serving many customers with logical isolation.
**Classic Data Plane:** Compute runs in the customer's cloud account, orchestrated by the control plane.
**Serverless Data Plane:** Compute runs in a Databricks-managed account; the control plane still orchestrates, but the compute layer is also Databricks-operated.
advantages: **Managed Experience:** Databricks handles upgrades, availability, and operation of the orchestration backend.
**Data Sovereignty (classic):** Customer data stays in the customer's cloud account, easing compliance.
**Centralized Governance:** Identity, permissions, audit logs, and metadata are managed centrally.
**Reduced Attack Surface:** Secure Cluster Connectivity allows clusters with no public IPs and no inbound ports.
disadvantages: **Dependency on Control Plane Availability:** Orchestration (new job/cluster launches, autoscaling) depends on control-plane reachability.
**Networking Complexity:** Connecting control plane and data plane securely (PrivateLink, peering, egress) adds configuration burden.
**Limited Visibility:** Customers cannot directly inspect or modify control-plane internals.
**Cross-Account Trust:** The control plane needs IAM roles/managed identities in the customer account to manage compute, requiring careful permission scoping.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: The control-plane/data-plane model is inherent to Databricks; embrace customer-managed VPC and PrivateLink when strict data isolation and compliance are required.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: If an organization cannot tolerate any vendor-managed orchestration layer or any cross-account IAM trust, a fully self-hosted Spark stack might be considered, at the cost of losing the managed platform benefits.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: The control plane is like an air traffic control tower: it sees all flights, issues takeoff/landing instructions, and coordinates schedules and metadata, but it never carries the passengers or cargo itself. The planes (clusters) and the cargo (data) live and move in the airspace and runways (the data plane).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Databricks stores all my data in its own cloud account.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In the classic architecture, your data stays in your own cloud storage and is processed by clusters in your own VPC/VNet. The control plane mostly handles metadata, code, and orchestration, plus small result previews.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the control plane goes down, all running jobs immediately fail.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Clusters already running can often continue executing in-flight work, but new orchestration actions (launching jobs/clusters, autoscaling, UI interaction) are impacted. Databricks runs the control plane with HA to minimize this.

productionConsiderations.scalability: The control plane is engineered by Databricks to scale orchestration and metadata across many workspaces; customers scale compute independently in the data plane by adjusting cluster sizes and autoscaling.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Databricks operates the control plane regionally with redundancy and SLAs; engineers should design pipelines with retries and idempotency to tolerate transient control-plane or relay disruptions.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Secure relay connections reconnect automatically; jobs have configurable retries. Mission-critical workloads should set retry policies and alerting so transient orchestration failures self-heal.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use the Databricks audit logs, system tables, and job/cluster event logs (delivered from the control plane) to monitor orchestration; integrate with cloud-native monitoring for data-plane VM health.
productionConsiderations.security: The boundary is enforced via scoped IAM roles/managed identities, encrypted control-plane-to-data-plane channels, optional PrivateLink, customer-managed keys, and Secure Cluster Connectivity; least-privilege scoping of the cross-account role is critical.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Terminate idle clusters via the control plane's auto-termination, use job (ephemeral) clusters rather than long-running all-purpose clusters, and right-size autoscaling to minimize data-plane VM cost.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep the control plane and data plane in the same cloud region to minimize relay latency; co-locate compute with storage in the data plane to reduce data-transfer latency and egress cost.

codeExamples.title: Creating a Job Cluster via the Jobs REST API (control-plane orchestration)
codeExamples.overview: This example calls the Databricks control-plane Jobs API to create a Workflow that launches an ephemeral job cluster in the customer's data plane and runs a notebook task.
codeExamples.breakdown: The request hits the control-plane Jobs API. The control plane stores the job definition and schedule as metadata. At trigger time, the cluster manager uses the supplied instance_profile_arn (an IAM role in the customer account) to launch VMs in the customer data plane, which then read/write the customer's data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A JSON response containing a job_id; the job appears in the Workflows UI and runs nightly at 02:00 UTC on an ephemeral cluster.
codeExamples.commonIssues: 401 errors from an invalid/expired token; cluster launch failures if the instance profile lacks permission to assume the role or access storage; using a node type unavailable in the region.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use job (ephemeral) clusters instead of all-purpose clusters to save cost; pin a Databricks runtime version for reproducibility; scope the instance profile to least privilege.

codeExamples.title: Configuring Secure Cluster Connectivity (no public IP) via Terraform
codeExamples.overview: This Terraform snippet configures a workspace network so data-plane clusters have no public IPs and connect outbound to the control plane only, hardening the boundary.
codeExamples.code:
resource "databricks_mws_networks" "this" {
  account_id   = var.databricks_account_id
  network_name = "prod-customer-managed-vpc"
  vpc_id       = aws_vpc.dbx.id
  subnet_ids   = [aws_subnet.private_a.id, aws_subnet.private_b.id]
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.dbx.id]
}

resource "databricks_mws_workspaces" "this" {
  account_id     = var.databricks_account_id
  workspace_name = "prod"
  aws_region     = "us-east-1"
  network_id     = databricks_mws_networks.this.network_id
  # Secure Cluster Connectivity: clusters have no public IP
  pricing_tier   = "ENTERPRISE"
}
codeExamples.breakdown: The customer-managed VPC places data-plane clusters in private subnets. With Secure Cluster Connectivity, clusters initiate outbound connections to the control-plane relay; no inbound ports or public IPs are needed, so the control plane never directly reaches into the cluster.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A workspace whose clusters launch into private subnets with no public IPs and connect to the control plane via the secure relay.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Clusters fail to launch if private subnets lack NAT/PrivateLink egress to reach the control plane and required endpoints; missing security group egress rules; insufficient IP space in subnets for autoscaling.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use AWS PrivateLink (or Azure Private Link) for control-plane connectivity to avoid public-internet egress; size subnets generously for autoscaling headroom.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A regulated financial firm wants a managed analytics platform but must guarantee that raw customer transaction data never leaves its own AWS account, while still using Databricks' UI, scheduling, and cluster management.
endToEndExample.inputData: Transaction files landing in the firm's S3 bucket (in its own AWS account); Databricks notebooks and job definitions authored in the workspace UI.
endToEndExample.architecture: A Databricks control plane (Databricks-managed, multi-tenant, in-region) orchestrates a classic data plane deployed into the firm's customer-managed VPC with Secure Cluster Connectivity and PrivateLink. Clusters use an instance profile to read/write the firm's S3 buckets.
processingSteps: 1. Engineers author a Bronze ingestion notebook in the workspace UI (stored in the control plane).
2. They create a Workflow (job) via the control-plane scheduler with a nightly cron trigger.
3. At trigger time, the cluster manager launches an ephemeral job cluster into the firm's private subnets (data plane).
4. The cluster reads transaction files directly from the firm's S3 using the instance profile, processes them, and writes Delta tables back to the firm's S3.
5. Only command instructions, run metadata, and small result previews traverse the control plane.
endToEndExample.output: Curated Delta tables stored entirely in the firm's S3, with job run history, audit logs, and metadata available in the control-plane UI.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Job run status and cluster events are surfaced from the control plane; audit logs and system tables track who ran what. Cloud-native CloudWatch metrics monitor data-plane VM and network health.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Workflow retry policies handle transient failures; if the control plane relay is briefly unreachable, in-flight cluster work continues and orchestration resumes on reconnect. Failed runs trigger alerts to on-call.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The firm gets a fully managed Databricks experience while keeping all raw and curated data inside its own AWS account, satisfying auditors that the SaaS vendor's control plane never stores transaction data.

industryUseCases.problem: Need a managed lakehouse but cannot allow a vendor to store sensitive financial data outside their cloud account.
industryUseCases.solution: Deploy classic data plane in a customer-managed VPC with PrivateLink and Secure Cluster Connectivity; the control plane handles only orchestration and metadata.
industryUseCases.benefits: Compliance with data residency and audit requirements while retaining the managed UI, scheduler, and cluster manager.

industryUseCases.problem: Patient data must remain within a controlled, encrypted environment with strict access boundaries.
industryUseCases.solution: Customer-managed VPC data plane with customer-managed encryption keys; control plane orchestrates clusters without storing PHI.
industryUseCases.benefits: HIPAA-eligible deployment where PHI stays in the customer account; clear control-plane/data-plane boundary simplifies audits.

industryUseCases.company: Global Retailers running large ETL fleets
industryUseCases.problem: Hundreds of nightly pipelines must be scheduled, retried, and monitored reliably across many teams.
industryUseCases.solution: The control-plane Job Scheduler (Workflows) orchestrates DAGs with dependencies, retries, and alerting while ephemeral job clusters scale in the data plane.
industryUseCases.benefits: Centralized, reliable orchestration with elastic compute and cost control via ephemeral clusters and auto-termination.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Databricks scales the multi-tenant control plane horizontally to orchestrate many workspaces and concurrent jobs; customers scale data-plane compute independently via cluster sizing and autoscaling, decoupling orchestration scale from processing scale.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Secure relay connections auto-reconnect; job/task retry policies and idempotent writes (Delta) ensure transient control-plane or network disruptions do not corrupt data. Running clusters can survive brief control-plane blips.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: The control plane runs with regional redundancy and a published SLA. Customers should deploy data-plane subnets across multiple availability zones so cluster autoscaling and recovery survive AZ failures.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Notebook code (via Repos/Git), job definitions (as code via Terraform/APIs), and data (Delta in customer storage with replication) should be version-controlled and replicated so a workspace can be reconstructed in another region if needed.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Co-locate control plane and data plane in the same region to minimize relay latency; co-locate compute with storage to cut data-access latency; use PrivateLink to avoid public-internet hops.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Use ephemeral job clusters, aggressive auto-termination of idle all-purpose clusters, autoscaling, and spot/preemptible instances for the data plane; remember the bill splits into Databricks DBUs plus underlying cloud VM/storage costs.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Scope the cross-account IAM role/managed identity to least privilege; enable Secure Cluster Connectivity (no public IPs), PrivateLink, customer-managed encryption keys, IP access lists for the UI, and SSO/SCIM for identity.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Leverage control-plane audit logs, system tables (billing, lineage, access), and job/cluster event logs; export to a SIEM. Pair with cloud-native metrics for data-plane VM/network observability.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Because the control plane only orchestrates, data quality enforcement (expectations, constraints) runs in the data plane within pipelines (e.g., Delta Live Tables expectations) and writes results to customer storage.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Configure job failure alerts and webhook/email notifications in the scheduler; centralize audit logs; alert on anomalous control-plane API usage (e.g., unexpected cluster creation) for security.

recommendedPractices: **Deploy a customer-managed VPC/VNet** for the classic data plane when isolation and compliance matter.
**Enable Secure Cluster Connectivity** so clusters have no public IPs and only outbound control-plane connectivity.
**Manage workspaces and jobs as code** (Terraform, APIs) so orchestration metadata is reproducible and version-controlled.
**Scope cross-account IAM roles to least privilege** so the control plane can manage compute but cannot over-reach into customer resources.
engineeringStandards: All production jobs must be defined via the control-plane Jobs/Workflows API with explicit retry and alerting policies.
Clusters must auto-terminate after a defined idle period to control cost.
Network configuration (subnets, security groups, PrivateLink) between control and data plane must be reviewed by security before production use.
designRecommendations: Keep control plane and data plane in the same cloud region to minimize latency and avoid cross-region egress.
Prefer ephemeral job clusters over long-running all-purpose clusters for scheduled pipelines.
Design pipelines to be idempotent so control-plane retries do not duplicate data.
namingConventions: Name workspaces by environment and region (e.g., prod-us-east-1).
Prefix job names by domain and cadence (e.g., bronze_ingest_daily).
Tag clusters with cost-center and team tags propagated to cloud VMs for billing attribution.
documentationStandards: Document the network topology showing control-plane relay, PrivateLink endpoints, and data-plane subnets.
Document the exact IAM role/managed identity permissions granted to the control plane.
Maintain a runbook describing behavior and recovery steps during a control-plane outage.
testingStrategies: Test cluster launch in private subnets to validate egress to the control plane (no public IP) before go-live.
Test job retry and alerting by injecting failures.
Validate that revoking the cross-account role correctly prevents cluster launches, confirming the boundary.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Databricks stores customer data in the control plane.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Conflating SaaS with full data hosting; not understanding the classic data-plane model.
commonMistakes.impact: Incorrect compliance posture and architecture decisions; unnecessary anxiety or, conversely, false assumptions in security reviews.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Recognize that in classic compute, data stays in the customer's account; the control plane handles metadata, code, and orchestration plus small result previews.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying clusters in private subnets without egress to the control plane.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Hardening the network without providing NAT or PrivateLink for the required outbound control-plane connectivity.
commonMistakes.impact: Clusters fail to launch or hang in PENDING because the data-plane agent cannot reach the control-plane relay.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Provide NAT gateway or PrivateLink endpoints for outbound control-plane connectivity and open the required egress rules.

commonMistakes.mistake: Over-permissioning the control plane's cross-account IAM role.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Granting broad admin permissions to avoid debugging access errors.
commonMistakes.impact: Expands blast radius and violates least privilege; security risk if the role were ever misused.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Grant only the permissions needed to manage compute and access designated storage; review and audit the role regularly.

comparisonSection.explanation: The control plane manages the UI, notebooks, job scheduling, cluster lifecycle, and metadata in Databricks' account. The data plane is where compute actually runs and customer data is processed and stored (customer account in classic).
Customer data does not reside in the control plane (only metadata, code, small previews). In classic deployments, data resides in the customer's cloud storage and is processed by data-plane clusters.

Databricks operates the control plane in its own cloud account. The classic data plane runs in the customer's cloud account under the customer's networking and IAM control; serverless data plane is Databricks-operated.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the Databricks control plane?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is the Databricks-managed backend, hosted in Databricks' own cloud account, that provides the workspace UI, notebooks, job scheduler, cluster manager, and metadata services. It orchestrates compute that runs in the data plane.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that it manages and orchestrates but, in classic compute, does not store or process customer data itself.

beginnerQuestions.question: Name three services that live in the control plane.
beginnerQuestions.answer: The workspace UI/notebooks, the job scheduler (Workflows), and the cluster manager. Metadata such as cluster configs, job definitions, and notebook code also lives there.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Listing concrete services shows you understand the control plane's responsibilities.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does the control plane orchestrate compute without holding customer data in classic deployments?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The cluster manager calls the cloud provider's compute API (using a scoped cross-account role) to launch VMs in the customer's account. Those VMs open a secure outbound connection back to the control plane and read/write data directly from the customer's cloud storage. Only commands, run metadata, and small result previews transit the control plane.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlight the secure relay and that data movement stays within the data plane.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is Secure Cluster Connectivity and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It is a mode where data-plane clusters have no public IPs and only outbound connectivity to the control-plane relay, with no inbound ports open. It reduces attack surface and is a common enterprise hardening requirement.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Connect it to the security boundary and network design between the planes.

advancedQuestions.question: Walk through the security boundary between control plane and data plane and how Databricks limits the control plane's access to customer data.
advancedQuestions.answer: Customer data lives in the data plane (customer cloud storage). The control plane is granted a scoped cross-account IAM role/managed identity only to manage compute and designated storage. Communication uses an encrypted secure relay initiated outbound from clusters (SCC). Customers can add PrivateLink, IP access lists, customer-managed keys, and customer-managed VPCs to further constrain access. The control plane stores metadata and small previews but not the bulk data, and customers can disable result downloads/previews for stricter isolation.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer ties together IAM scoping, networking (SCC/PrivateLink), encryption keys, and what metadata vs. data the control plane sees.

advancedQuestions.question: What happens to running jobs and the platform if the control plane becomes temporarily unreachable?
advancedQuestions.answer: Clusters already running can often continue executing in-flight tasks because compute and data live in the data plane. However, new orchestration actions, launching jobs or clusters, autoscaling decisions, and UI interactions, are impacted until connectivity is restored. Databricks runs the control plane with regional HA to minimize this, and retry/idempotency in pipelines protects against transient disruptions.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you understand the failure domain split between orchestration and execution.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A security team insists no customer data ever leaves the company's AWS account, but they still want Databricks notebooks and scheduling. How do you design this?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Separate orchestration (control plane) from data processing (data plane). Keep data in the customer's S3, run a classic data plane in a customer-managed VPC, harden with SCC and PrivateLink, scope the cross-account role, and optionally disable result downloads.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Deploy a classic data plane in a customer-managed VPC with private subnets, Secure Cluster Connectivity (no public IPs), and PrivateLink to the control plane. Use an instance profile scoped to the company's S3 buckets. The control plane provides UI, notebooks, and scheduling but only handles metadata and small previews; bulk data never leaves the account. Add customer-managed keys and IP access lists for defense in depth.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a multi-team Databricks deployment for a regulated enterprise emphasizing the control-plane/data-plane boundary.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use per-environment workspaces (dev/stage/prod) each on a Databricks-managed control plane in-region. Deploy classic data planes into customer-managed VPCs with SCC and PrivateLink. Centralize identity via SSO/SCIM and governance via Unity Catalog. Manage workspaces, networks, and jobs as code with Terraform.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Customer-managed VPC and PrivateLink add networking complexity but maximize isolation. Serverless reduces management but moves compute to Databricks' account, which some compliance regimes may restrict. Ephemeral job clusters cut cost but add startup latency.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Scale orchestration via the multi-tenant control plane (Databricks-managed); scale compute via autoscaling and additional job clusters in the data plane. Spread subnets across AZs and ensure sufficient IP space for autoscaling headroom.

Notebook code, job definitions, run history, and cluster configs are control-plane metadata.
Keep both planes in the same region to minimize relay latency and avoid egress cost.
Use ephemeral job clusters and auto-termination to control data-plane cost.

keyTakeaways: The control plane is Databricks' managed backend (workspace UI, notebooks, job scheduler, cluster manager, metadata) running in Databricks' own cloud account.

It orchestrates compute that runs in the data plane; in the classic architecture customer data stays in the customer's cloud account and only metadata, code, and small previews touch the control plane.

The control-plane/data-plane split, hardened with Secure Cluster Connectivity, PrivateLink, scoped IAM roles, and customer-managed VPCs, is the foundation of Databricks' enterprise security and compliance story.

Running clusters can survive brief control-plane disruptions, but new orchestration (launching jobs/clusters, autoscaling) depends on control-plane availability, so design pipelines with retries and idempotency.
Costs split between Databricks DBUs (platform) and underlying cloud VM/storage in the data plane, so co-locating planes in one region and using ephemeral clusters optimizes both latency and spend.
